title: Integration as Area Under a Curve: Visualizing the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
pedagogical_goal: This simulation demonstrates why integration calculates the area under a curve by visualizing the accumulation of infinitesimal rectangles under a function f(x). Users will explore how the definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx represents the net signed area between the curve and the x-axis, and how this process is the inverse of differentiation through the Fundamental Theorem of Calculus.

fundamental_laws: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus: If F(x) is an antiderivative of f(x), then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a)
The definite integral ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx represents the limit of Riemann sums: lim (n→∞) Σ f(xᵢ*) Δx where Δx = (b-a)/n
For a velocity function v(t), the displacement over [a,b] is ∫ₐᵇ v(t) dt, demonstrating the area-under-curve interpretation in physics

derived_formulas.riemann_sum: Array.from({length: n_rectangles}, (_, i) => { const xi = a + i * rectangle_width; return function_value * rectangle_width; }).reduce((sum, val) => sum + val, 0)

components.description: X and Y axes with tick marks and labels. X-axis from x=-6 to x=6, Y-axis from y=-4 to y=4. Drawn as two perpendicular lines with arrowheads. Includes grid lines every 0.5 units for reference.

The function f(x) plotted as a smooth curve. For linear: f(x)=x; quadratic: f(x)=x²; sine: f(x)=sin(x). Stroke: accent color, width: 3px. The curve is sampled at 100 points between x=-6 and x=6 to ensure smoothness.

A series of rectangles representing the Riemann sum approximation. Each rectangle has width = (b-a)/n_rectangles and height = f(x_i) where x_i is the left endpoint. Fill: primary color with 0.4 opacity, stroke: primary color, width: 1px. Rectangles are only drawn between x=a and x=b.

The exact area under the curve between x=a and x=b, filled with secondary color at 0.3 opacity. This shape is generated by sampling the function at 50 points between a and b, then closing the path down to the x-axis and back to the start point.

The antiderivative F(x) plotted as a dashed curve when show_antiderivative is enabled. For linear: F(x)=x²/2; quadratic: F(x)=x³/3; sine: F(x)=-cos(x). Stroke: accent color, width: 2px, dash array: '6,4'. Shown only if show_antiderivative = 1.

pedagogical_callouts.title: The Area Problem
pedagogical_callouts.text: We want to find the area under the curve f(x) between x=a and x=b. Simple geometry works for rectangles and triangles, but not for arbitrary curves. Integration solves this by summing infinitely many infinitesimally thin rectangles.

pedagogical_callouts.title: Riemann Sums: Building the Approximation
pedagogical_callouts.text: We approximate the area by dividing [a,b] into n rectangles. Each rectangle has width Δx = (b-a)/n and height f(x_i). As n increases (more rectangles), the approximation improves. The Riemann sum Σ f(x_i)Δx approaches the true area as n→∞.

pedagogical_callouts.title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus
pedagogical_callouts.text: Integration and differentiation are inverse processes. If F(x) is an antiderivative of f(x) (meaning F'(x)=f(x)), then the exact area under f(x) from a to b is F(b)-F(a). This is why we can compute areas using antiderivatives instead of limits of sums.

pedagogical_callouts.title: Signed Area and Physical Interpretation
pedagogical_callouts.text: The integral gives net signed area: area above the x-axis is positive, below is negative. In physics, if f(x) represents velocity, then ∫v(t)dt gives displacement. The area under the velocity curve equals the change in position.
